episodes.184589: Cold temperatures aloft due to the upper level low and lingering moisture combined with diurnal heating and sea breezes produced isolated strong to severe storms and locally heavy rainfall.
episodes.184743: Localized flash flooding was observed after a slow moving front brought multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms across Massachusetts into southern New Hampshire. The airmass was very moist and supported rainfall rates over 2 inches per hour.
episodes.184876: Out ahead of a cold front during the last very warm and humid day of a recent stretch of hot weather, thunderstorms developed mid to late afternoon from central Pennsylvania to central New York. A line of severe storms developed in this area and lifted north across the Finger Lakes and eventually the eastern Lake Ontario region. Several reports of wind damage were received as these storms moved through, especially over Oswego and Lewis counties.
episodes.185137: Between 9:15 p.m. CDT on Thursday the 7th and 12:30 a.m. CDT on Friday the 8th, the southern reaches of a fairly compact mesoscale convective system (MCS) brushed through far northern sections of South Central Nebraska, primarily affecting Valley, Greeley, Nance, northeast Merrick and Polk counties. Along the vast majority of its journey across these local counties, this MCS was pretty tame, producing only brief rainfall and sub-severe wind gusts no more than 40-50 MPH. However, one notable exception of more intense/severe winds was detected by automated sensors at the Ord airport, where at 9:44 p.m. CDT the official ASOS clocked a rogue gust of 78 MPH while a nearly co-located Nebraska Mesonet station peaked at 63 MPH. As evidence of the very isolated nature of these severe gusts, there were no ground-truth reports of wind damage within the town of Ord itself, and the only other 50+ MPH gust detected within the local area during this event was 51 MPH in western Nance County (unofficial mesonet). ||This overwhelmingly sub-severe MCS originated as initially-isolated convection over southwest South Dakota and northwest Nebraska during the afternoon and early evening, before growing upscale with time over north central Nebraska and grazing the northern reaches of South Central Nebraska. Within the local area, convection first rolled through Valley/Greeley counties mainly 9:15-10:30 p.m. CDT, crossed Nance County during the ensuing hour and exited Polk County by 12:30 a.m. CDT. Some trailing redevelopment flared up over mainly Polk County 1-2 hours later but was non-severe. In the mid-upper levels, west-northwesterly flow prevailed over the Central Plains, with a low amplitude shortwave trough tracking across the heart of Nebraska during the evening and supporting moderately strong deep-layer wind shear around 40 knots. The main limiting factor to a more robust severe weather threat was limited low-level moisture and instability, with evening surface dewpoints in the Ord area only mid-50s (F) and most-unstable CAPE no higher than 500-1000 J/kg.
episodes.185150: An upper level disturbance and cold front moved across a moderately unstable airmass due to near record warmth across VT. Scattered thunderstorms developed during the afternoon, some of which produced locally damaging winds.
episodes.185240: Strong to severe thunderstorms developed across much of northwestern Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 8th, as lift north of a warm front increased as an upper level disturbance translated into the area. The strongest thunderstorms produced hail up to nickel size and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.185253: A stationary front provided the focus for the development of slow moving heavy thunderstorms on the afternoon of September 8th 2023. The thunderstorms developed in an unstable environment with CAPE values of 3000-4000 J/kg and PWATs near 1.7 - 1.8 inches. These thunderstorms produced rainfall rates of 1-2 inches per hour with a total accumulation of 1-3 inches of rain.
episodes.185255: A stationary front provided the focus for the development of slow moving heavy thunderstorms on the afternoon of September 8th 2023. episodes.185489: A circulation developed southwest of the Marianas on September 6th  and then lifted northwest, passing through the Marianas and was west of the Marianas by September 8th. This led to southwest flow and periods of heavy rain across the Guam, leading to flooding across southern portions of Guam.
episodes.185531: Scattered thunderstorms developed along an advancing surface cold front across the Red River Valley during the afternoon of the 8th. Strong convective potential instability and marginally sufficient deep-layer (organizing) wind shear allowed for transient storm organization (into supercells). A few reports of wind and hail were received associated with the strongest thunderstorms.
episodes.185574: Morning sea breeze thunderstorms enhanced by a surface trough moving across central Florida produce gusty winds across Tampa Bay neighboring waters.
episodes.185620: Scattered severe thunderstorms in advance of a frontal boundary produced damaging winds and large hail across portions of central and south central Virginia.
episodes.185635: Isolated severe storms produced hail up to quarters in size.
episodes.185638: Isolated thunderstorms developed over the Pine Ridge of South Dakota during the early evening hours of September 7th. As this isolated thunderstorm activity tracked to the east-southeast, thunderstorm coverage increased over north central Nebraska. Some storms were severe with hail up to half dollar size and wind gusts up to 60 MPH.
episodes.185641: A lee trough east of the North Carolina Appalachians amid a warm and moist atmosphere led to the development of widely isolated showers and storms over the central North Carolina Piedmont in the evening hours. A few storms produced quarter-size hail and damaging winds over Stanly, Anson, and Granville Counties.
episodes.185642: An upper-level trough over the southern Appalachians combined with a surface trough over the eastern Piedmont and an inland penetrating sea breeze to produce scattered showers and thunderstorms over the eastern Sandhills, Coastal Plain, and eastern Piedmont. Several of the storms produced damaging winds and hail along and east of the US-1 Corridor.
episodes.185663: A few thunderstorms developed and moved through the Coastal Plain counties of Eastern NC during the afternoon hours. One such storm became severe and produced damaging winds.
episodes.185685: Scattered thunderstorms in advance of a frontal boundary produced heavy rain which caused flash flooding across portions of central Virginia.
episodes.185686: Scattered severe thunderstorms in advance of a frontal boundary produced damaging winds across portions of central and south central Virginia.
episodes.185687: Isolated severe thunderstorm in advance of a frontal boundary produced damaging winds across portions of northeast North Carolina.
episodes.185717: Widely scattered thunderstorms developed across the Coastal Plain during the afternoon and tracked eastwards. One of these storms produced damaging winds across the northern Sounds.
episodes.185759: A frontal boundary and low pressure system located to the west and east of eastern New York was the focus for rounds of showers and thunderstorms each day September 7-9. Strong to severe thunderstorms were more widespread on September 7-8. These storms resulted in numerous reports of tree and powerline damage, as well as thousands without power and several road closures.
episodes.185768: An area of scattered thunderstorms with heavy rain and hail ranging in size from dimes to quarters moved across much of the Flint Hills and into Southeast Kansas.  There were some isolated reports of quarter sized hail in Elk and Montgomery counties but most of the hail was sub severe. Rainfall amounts of 0.50 inches to 1.28 inches were reported from these storms but no flooding occurred as the ground was very dry prior to the arrival of the thunderstorm activity.
episodes.185794: A cold front and upper trough slowly approached the area on September 7th, providing a source of lift for the pre-existing instability generated by diurnal heating across southern and central Virginia. This combination created an atmosphere that was conducive for damaging winds gusts. Around 2900 people were left without power in Roanoke, and another 655 were without power in Henry County.
episodes.185802: A cold front and upper trough slowly approached the area on September 7th, providing a source of lift for the pre-existing instability generated by diurnal heating across northwest North Carolina. This combination created an atmosphere that was conducive for damaging winds gusts.
episodes.185813: A weak surface trough moved into the area. This feature moved into a very unstable airmass as it was a hot and humid day. Strong to severe thunderstorms developed, producing large hail and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.185814: A weak surface trough moved into the area. This feature moved into a very unstable airmass as it was a hot and humid day. Strong to severe thunderstorms developed, producing large hail and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.185815: With continued southwesterly flow aloft, another disturbance moved through, into a hot, humid, and unstable airmass. This resulted in the development of strong to severe thunderstorms in parts of New Jersey, which produced damaging wind gusts and large hail.
episodes.185816: With continued southwesterly flow aloft, another disturbance moved through, into a hot, humid, and unstable airmass. This resulted in the development of strong to severe thunderstorms in parts of eastern Pennsylvania, which produced damaging wind gusts and large hail.
episodes.185817: With continued southwesterly flow aloft, another disturbance moved through, into a hot, humid, and unstable airmass. This resulted in the development of strong to severe thunderstorms in parts of Delaware, which produced large hail.
episodes.185871: A stationary front positioned roughly from New York to the Gulf Coast led to several rounds of showers and thunderstorms in the Piedmont of Virginia. An upper level storm system combined with daytime heating helped increased the coverage of storms during the afternoon and evening hours, while low level convergence along the front focused the thunderstorm activity near the mountains.
episodes.185975: A small cluster of thunderstorms developed early in the morning on September 8th across parts of Southern Arkansas. This activity was tied to warm and moist advection associated with a west-southwesterly low-level jet across the Southern Plains. Outflow boundaries from these thunderstorms quickly surged southward and well ahead of the leading edge of convection. A moist low-level air mass was present downstream of this convection and the onset of daytime heating of this moist air mass gradually eroded convective inhibition in concert with gradually increasing MLCAPE. As a result, a few instances of damaging wind gusts were reported across Hempstead and Nevada Counties.
episodes.186110: A convective cloud line developed over and just north of the Lower Florida Keys, producing a family of waterspouts and one strong thunderstorm.
episodes.186123: A pair of shortwaves moved across central and south central Louisiana during the afternoons of the 7th and 8th. While only a couple thunderstorms occurred on the 7th, a southward traveling line of severe weather developed on the second day.
episodes.186136: An upper level disturbance passed through the region during early September causing a southward moving line of storms.
episodes.186138: A shortwave moved south across Louisiana and East Texas and over the gulf waters. This disturbance allowed a line of severe storms to move into the nearshore gulf waters of Louisiana.
episodes.186165: During the afternoon and evening, a cold front came through the area. It triggered many storms along it as it moved through. Ample instability and mid-level dry air aided the stronger storms in the complex to produce damaging winds before it pushed through the area.

episodes.186202: An anomalously warm and humid airmass was in place across the state of New Hampshire on September 7th with high temperatures well into the 80s along with surface moisture.  This allowed for high instability values to develop through the day.  A weak frontal boundary began  to approach Western new Hampshire by the evening where a few lines of thunderstorms developed and slowly moved into the Connecticut River Valley.  A few isolated storms became severe with large hail and damaging winds, but overall the damage was sporadic and mostly confided near the Vermont border near the Connecticut River Valley.
episodes.186205: An anomalously warm and humid airmass was in place across the state of Maine on September 7th with high temperatures well into the 80s along with surface moisture. This allowed for high instability values to develop through the day. A weak frontal boundary began to approach the Quebec and Maine border by the evening where a few storms developed.  A discrete line of storms developed in Somerset County where one storm briefly became severe bringing damaging wind gusts.
episodes.186206: A strong mid-level trough ejected out of New York and pushed from southwest to northeast across New England during the day on September 8th.  This feature had ample low level instability to work with as the region was experiencing well above normal temperatures and moisture for early September.  All these ingredients came together to bring a line of severe thunderstorms to the area with strong damaging straight-line wind gusts being the primary hazard.

events.narrative: A family of four waterspouts was observed north of Key West by NWS employees and the contract weather observer at NAS Key West Boca Chica Field.  Two spray rings were observed via the NWS rooftop cameras. One waterspout consisted of a very narrow, nearly-vertical condensation cloud extending almost completely from the cloud base to the surface.  The second waterspout was very wide with its condensation cloud extending about one-quarter the way from cloud base.  The remaining two waterspouts were nearly vertical, very narrow, with condensation clouds not extending very far from cloud base.  The waterspouts moved toward the west around 5 knots.
